name: AI/Engagement 2 Internal REVIEWED
content:
# Workshop 2
 
 # Different AI Horses for Different Courses: Matching Tools to Purpose
 
 **Speakers:** [Greta Ríos](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/staff-and-boards/greta-rios) (Co-Executive Director, People Powered) and [Nikhil Kumar](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/staff-and-boards/nikhil-kumar) (Resource Manager, People Powered)
 
 [People Powered](https:/www.peoplepowered.org) is a global hub for participatory democracy that supports government and civil society organizations in implementing participatory practices effectively. In this session, they present their updated [Guide to Digital Participation Platforms](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/digital-guide-home) , including an AI-focused section developed in partnership with Matt Stempeck ( [Civic Tech Field Guide](https:/civictech.guide) ), UNDP, and the Friedrich Naumann Foundation.
 
 The session offers a practical definition of AI for participation, a principle-first approach to responsible use, concrete risks and opportunities, a before/during/after map of where AI can help, and a framework for selecting platforms and AI features.
 
 ## 
 
 ## Defining AI for participation and establishing principles
 
 Kumar frames AI as an umbrella term for technologies that let computers do things humans would otherwise do. What counts as "AI" shifts over time — tools like speech processing were once "AI" but are now taken for granted. For this guide, "AI" includes natural language processing, machine learning, and generative AI (LLMs).
 
 People Powered developed an [organizational AI policy](https:/docs.google.com/document/d/1oMD9nTZ4aaCrBBcBKX0QhzeaNdOa-MsvtYEd5JsT4-4/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.fxii2nqoi5sm) grounded in values: mission alignment (AI serves democratic goals), human-centeredness (technology supports human agency), transparency (clear how AI works and how decisions are calculated), accountability (humans remain responsible for outputs), sustainability (considering environmental impact), equity and inclusion (addressing bias and digital divides), continuous learning, and privacy and security.
 
 Kumar encourages practitioners to "work with the communities that power your work, and the stakeholders that you engage with, to develop your own set of principles to guide your approach, so that it is grounded in your values, and so that you're not just reacting to the latest technology that's being developed."
 
 ## Concerns and opportunities from the field
 
 Kumar acknowledges [legitimate concerns](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/digital-guide/challenges-ai-presents) practitioners raise: lack of transparency in AI-assisted decisions, accountability gaps when humans do not filter outputs, economic consequences and job displacement in governance, harm to critical thinking and removal of the "human element" from participation, hallucination and sycophancy (retrieval-augmented generation can help mitigate these, but there are no perfect solutions), environmental impact (water, energy, inequitable siting of data centers), unknown second-order effects, and potential existential risks.
 
 At the same time, [concrete benefits are emerging from global practice.](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/digital-guide/ai-opportunities-for-participation) These include: efficiency gains that enable more participatory programs even with limited budgets, deeper engagement through new methods that bring in new people, reduced digital barriers (speech-to-text for those uncomfortable typing), more legible inputs through faster and more accurate analysis, and better sense-making from large-scale processes.
 
 The speakers' position is that concerns should inform design rather than prevent use.
 
 ## Practical application: lifecycle mapping and tool selection
 
 The speakers organized AI applications around the participation lifecycle.
 
 Before a process, AI can streamline administrative work, train staff, form diverse participant groups for citizens' assemblies, simulate participation to test platforms, and power dynamic FAQ tools.
 
 During a process, AI can parse, summarize, and classify contributions to support open-ended qualitative questions; transcribe speech to text ( [as in the Siegen-Wittgenstein district example using DeliberAIde](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/news-content/digital-participation-case-study-germany) ); assist participants through bots; and provide translation for multilingual accessibility.
 
 After a process, AI supports sense-making and analysis, written summaries, and analytics.
 
 For tool selection, Ríos and Kumar recommend starting with purpose and constraints rather than features: map goals for the process (participant outcomes, policy outcomes), assess resources (finances, staff time, technical capacity), establish AI principles before considering tools, identify needs from both participant and program manager perspectives, and only then select features that meet those needs.
 
 Their [updated guide](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/digital-guide-home) rates 30 digital participation tools on platform cost, capacity requirements, features, accessibility, ethics and transparency, and track record.
 
 ## Takeaways for learners
 
 Start with participatory goals and work backward to the tools, rather than adopting AI just because it is "flashy." As Kumar put it: “Think about the tool in service of your participatory process, rather than trying to make your participatory process fit into the new tool.”
 
 Develop principles to guide platform selections. Principles keep practitioners grounded in values instead of reacting to the newest tool.
 
 Language limitations matter. AI models trained on high-resource languages may underperform for communities speaking less common languages.
 
 Combine human facilitation and digital tools. The [Northern Ireland “Voice Matters” case](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/news-content/digital-participation-case-study-ireland) demonstrates technology "being used in service of the participatory process" rather than replacing human elements. [Dembrane](https:/www.dembrane.com) speech capture freed facilitators to focus on in-person engagement.
 
 ## Audience notes
 
 ### 
 
 ### Poll results
 
 Across digital platforms, the audience was evenly split: 33% had used them 3 or more times, 25% once or twice, 33% never, and 9% unsure.
 
 On AI specifically, the numbers were more striking: 67% said they had not used AI features to support participatory processes, while only 19% had used AI to prepare for a process, 3% during, and 3% after.
 
 ### 
 
 ### Questions
 
 Does the guide address mixing synchronous and asynchronous participation features?
 
 Can we get recommendations on when/how AI tools are used in a process to allow sufficient opportunity for human review of products to ensure accuracy and appropriateness?
 
 ### Locations and affiliations
 
 The session drew participants from across the US: New Jersey (NJ DMAHS Preventive Health; NJ Office of Innovation AI for Impact Fellow), Sacramento (California High-Speed Rail Authority), Montgomery County MD (Arts & Humanities Council), Portland OR (Portland State University doctoral research on sense-making in infrastructure planning), Kansas City MO, Cambridge MA (Allen Lab for Democracy Renovation, Harvard Kennedy School), Washington DC (George Mason University Enterprise Center; tech-public sector bridge work), Idaho, Stillwater OK, South Philadelphia, New York, San Diego, Florida, Honolulu, Anchorage, Washington State, Jefferson County, Silicon Valley (Better Together America SV / Thriving Together US), and Colorado. International participants joined from Sweden (community/nature design), Mexico (Aceleradora de Ciudades, working with 20 municipalities), Madrid, Athens, Budapest (local ecosystem development, infrastructure funds), Cape Town (Technology for Good), Tel Aviv, Armenia, Ubatuba (Brazil), and Luxembourg.
 
 ## Quotes
 
 ### 
 
 ### Greta Ríos (People Powered)
 
 "We think that we need to create ways to make sure that every voice counts, because when people participate in decision making, we have better policies and we have stronger results."
 
 "Participatory democracy is hard, and if it's not done correctly, it can be even harmful."
 
 "People Powered exists because we want to expand people's power to make government decisions."
 
 ### Nikhil Kumar (People Powered)
 
 "Think about the tool in service of your participatory process, rather than trying to make your participatory process fit into the shiny new tool."
 
 "I would also encourage all of you to work with the communities that power your work, and the stakeholders that you engage with, to develop your own set of principles to guide your approach, so that it is grounded in your values, and so that you're not just reacting to the latest technology that's being developed."
 
 "A lot of AIs are trained on high-resource languages. But if there are languages that are less commonly represented in tech, then the AI might not be as useful."
 
 ## Platforms/Tools/Resources
 
 [People Powered Guide to Digital Participation Platforms](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/digital-guide-home) — Comprehensive guidance on selecting, setting up, and running digital participation tools. Updated 2025 with a new AI section.
 
 [People Powered Platform Ratings](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/platform-ratings) — Analysis of 30 digital participation tools rated on cost, capacity requirements, features, accessibility, ethics/transparency, and track record.
 
 [Civic Tech Field Guide](https:/civictech.guide) — Maintained by Matt Stempeck, who collaborated on the guide.
 
 [IdeaScale AI](https:/ideascale.com/ideascale-ai) — Provides AI guidance for designing innovation campaigns.
 
 [DeliberAIde case study](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/news-content/digital-participation-case-study-germany) — AI tool for participatory planning, includes speech-to-text (used in Siegen-Wittgenstein, Germany).
 
 [PopVox Staff Link, example of dynamic FAQ](https:/www.popvox.org/blog/stafflink) — Tool designed specifically for Congressional staff.
 
 [AssemblyAI](https:/www.assemblyai.com/docs/speech-understanding/summarization) — AI-generated summaries in creative formats.
 
 [Jigsaw Sensemaker](https:/jigsaw-code.github.io/sensemaking-tools) — Google product for sense-making from input.
 
 [Dembrane case study](https:/www.peoplepowered.org/news-content/digital-participation-case-study-ireland) — Speech capture tool used in Northern Ireland Voice Matters Initiative.
